sections.html:
On most Texas homes, a foreclosure is a courthouse auction run by the lender after a sequence of notices, without a lawsuit. This is nonjudicial foreclosure, and it rests on the power of sale in the deed of trust.

Judicial foreclosure exists but is uncommon. Home equity loans, reverse mortgages and owners' association assessment liens must go through an expedited court order instead. Your loan papers tell you which route applies.

On most home loans, federal rules prevent the servicer from beginning foreclosure until you are more than 120 days behind. That leaves a stretch of time to talk with the servicer before any formal notice shows up.

Texas also puts a clock on the lender. Civil Practice and Remedies Code section 16.035 sets a four-year limitations period for foreclosure actions, with exceptions. If you are holding an old default notice, ask an attorney whether that period matters.

Two notices drive the process, and each one starts a deadline.

  • Notice of default: you can reinstate by paying the past-due amount within 20 days of receiving it (Property Code section 51.002(d)).
  • Notice of sale: sent after the 20 days pass, with 21 days or more before the auction.
  • Posting and filing: the notice of sale goes on the courthouse door and to the county clerk, who charges $2.00 per notice under the 2023 clerk manual.
  • Military statement: the notice has to include the active-duty military statement.

Save every letter and write down the postmark.

Sales are held on the first Tuesday of the month, shifting to the Wednesday when that Tuesday is New Year's Day or Independence Day. The window runs from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and bidding starts at the time in the notice or within three hours after it.

The auction takes place at a location inside the property's own county. The commissioners court chooses it and records it in the real property records.

Foreclosure timeline at a glance
EventTiming
Federal start limitOver 120 days delinquent
ReinstatementWithin 20 days of default notice
Notice of saleAt least 21 days before the sale
AuctionFirst Tuesday of the month
Deficiency suitTwo years after the sale
Claim for excess tax-sale proceeds2 years from the sale

sections.h2: Where the money and the debt go
sections.html:
The bid pays the foreclosing lender first. Anything left over goes to junior lienholders and then to the former owner.

If the bid falls short, the lender can sue for the difference, but a deficiency suit has to be filed within two years of the sale. You can ask the court for a fair market value offset. After a property tax foreclosure sale, the former owner has two years from the sale to claim excess proceeds.

sections.h2: Can you redeem the house after foreclosure?
sections.html:
Generally no, not after a deed of trust sale. Redemption rights apply to narrow situations such as certain tax liens and owners' association assessment liens.

For a tax sale, the Texas Supreme Court has described Tax Code section 34.21 as follows. Homestead, agricultural and mineral interest property can be redeemed for two years after the purchaser's deed is filed, with a premium of 25 percent in the first year or 50 percent in the second. Other property can be redeemed by the 180th day after filing, with a premium of no more than 25 percent. The owner also repays the purchaser's bid and the added charges the opinion lists.

Write to the servicer early so you have a paper trail. Each option below races the auction date.

  • Reinstate within the 20-day cure period.
  • Request a repayment plan or modification from the servicer.
  • Sell the home before the first Tuesday sale.
  • Contact legal aid or a Texas attorney about your notices.

A sale ahead of the auction pays off the lien and keeps a trustee's deed out of the county records. Collect your default notice, sale notice and loan statements before you speak with a buyer. A cash buyer can often close fast because there is no lender underwriting or appraisal to wait on.

sections.h2: Foreclosure paperwork at the county level
sections.html:
Texas has 254 counties, and each county clerk keeps its own foreclosure record. The clerk records deeds of trust, liens and notices of foreclosure sale, and also serves as clerk of the commissioners court.

That second job helps you, because the commissioners court designates where sales happen. If you cannot tell where an auction will take place, ask the clerk. Rural and urban offices apply the same law but differ in hours and in how notices can be searched.

  • Contact the clerk where the house is located, not where you live.
  • Ask for the current list of posted notices of sale.
  • Ask where the commissioners court designated the sale area.
  • Ask how filings are accepted and what the fee will be.

Put everything about the loan in one folder before you speak with a servicer, an attorney or a buyer. With the dates in front of you, the nearest deadline is easy to spot.

  • The note and deed of trust from closing.
  • The notice of default and its envelope or delivery record.
  • The notice of sale and the date printed on it.
  • Recent loan statements and any servicer letters.
  • Proof of homestead use if you live in the house.

If property taxes are behind, remember that each year's tax lien arises on the first of January and a lender may pay the taxes and add them to your balance. Ask your servicer how taxes are being handled.

sections.h2: Why the dates on your notices matter
sections.html:
Each protection a Texas borrower has hangs on a date printed on a piece of paper. The cure period starts when the default letter arrives, and the auction cannot be held until the sale letter has aged enough. Mark each date on a calendar the day the mail comes.

If something looks wrong, such as a sale date that is not a Tuesday or a county other than the one where the house sits, tell the servicer in writing and see an attorney quickly. Small errors in timing or place can matter, and your window closes at the auction.

Keep a simple log: the date each letter was received, who sent it, and what it demanded. If you later sell or negotiate with the servicer, that log answers most of the questions anyone will ask.

sections.h2: If someone is still in the house after the sale
sections.html:
An auction buyer who finds an occupant may need an eviction case to get possession. The notice and justice court steps are on this site's eviction pages.

Allow for that gap. The buyer holds title at the auction but not automatic possession, and a seller who stays past the sale can expect a notice to vacate.

faqs.q: Is foreclosure in Texas judicial or nonjudicial?
faqs.a: Mostly nonjudicial, using the power of sale in the deed of trust. Home equity loans, reverse mortgages and some association liens need an expedited court order.

faqs.q: What is the reinstatement deadline on a Texas loan?
faqs.a: Twenty days from receipt of the default notice. Pay the past-due balance in that period, as section 51.002(d) of the Property Code provides.

faqs.q: How much notice comes before a Texas foreclosure sale?
faqs.a: At least 21 days. The notice must be posted on the courthouse door and filed with the clerk.

faqs.q: Can the lender still sue me after the auction?
faqs.a: Yes, for a shortfall, if it files a deficiency suit within two years of the sale. You may request a fair market value offset.

faqs.q: What day are Texas foreclosure auctions held?
faqs.a: The first Tuesday of each month. When that Tuesday falls on January 1 or July 4, the first Wednesday is used instead.
